scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Koothu originated in the early Tamilakam and has been practiced in Tamil Nadu since the Sangam period.
Classical Sangam literature such as the Silappatikaram contains detailed descriptions of the art form.
Developed as a folk medium combining drama, narrative, dance, and song, it emerged as both communal entertainment and a way to educate rural populations about religious lore and historical events.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Staged primarily during community festivals, Koothu performances are commonly dedicated to Hindu goddesses such as Mariamman or Draupadi.
Dramas draw upon episodes from Hindu epics including the Ramayana and Mahabharata, alongside wider mythology and regional folklore.
Beyond serving as festival entertainment, Koothu carries deep educational and religious significance, transmitting cultural heritage across generations.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Koothu is danced as street theatre in open public areas like village squares and temple grounds.
Dancers enact scenes through play performance, narration, and singing, executing turns that cause their swirling skirts to billow outward.
Footwork relies on the weight of heavy anklets sounding against the earth.
Watch for Skirt Swirl, Anklet Strike.

Formation: Open public spaces, village squares, or temple grounds; arranged either in mobile procession or on a fixed outdoor performance area

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Koothu is accompanied by traditional musical instruments that provide rhythmic and melodic support for singing and dramatic dialogue.
Musicians work alongside the kattiyakaran, who delivers narration from the background while the koothar sing and speak their roles.
Listen for the traditional instruments.

Live traditional instruments accompany vibrant vocal delivery, where actors alternate between spoken dialogue and sung passages while a background narrator, the kattiyakaran, anchors the theatrical storytelling.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The performers wear elaborate wooden headgear, prominent face paint, and detailed stage make-up to denote divine, heroic, or demonic roles.
Costumes feature swirling skirts tailored to accentuate spinning movements, accessorised by heavy ornaments including metal anklets.
Performances traditionally occur outdoors in open public spaces, temple courtyards, or village clearings, often illuminated for overnight stagings.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Performers are traditionally trained in theatre workshops known as koothu pattarai under the instruction of a teacher called a nattuvanar.
Contemporary institutional custodians include the Koothu-P-Pattarai theater group and the Kattaikuthu Gurukulam, which provides structured training for younger generations of artisans.
Major forms include Terukuttu, which denotes mobile street performances, and Kattaikkuttu, denoting stationary overnight narrative plays.
Tracing back to the Sangam period of early Tamilakam, Koothu represents one of the oldest continuing dramatic lineages in South Asia.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Koothu is variant of Koodiyattam: Performed in Kerala in combination with Sanskrit theatre forms and Chakyar Koothu.
Koothu is variant of Chakyar Koothu: A Kerala theatrical tradition sharing historical and conceptual roots with Koothu.
Koothu is sibling of Kathakali: A fellow South Indian dance-theatre tradition sharing dramatic epic themes and elaborate facial makeup.
Koothu is sibling of Yakshagana: A related regional folk-theatre tradition incorporating epic narratives, prominent headgear, and dance.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Koothu performances are often sacred community rituals dedicated to Hindu deities such as Mariamman and Draupadi during temple festivals, requiring traditional ceremonial respect and adherence to local ritual codes.
